title: Architecture & Standards: Unified Guidelines and ADR Process
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards: API, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and the Decision Record (ADR) process. It is intended as the canonical reference for architects, platform engineers, serving-runtime teams, and service owners when designing or updating services and runtimes.

Scope

- Applies to all public and internal services, runtime components, deployment manifests, and ADRs for architecture/infrastructure/model-serving decisions.
- Excludes one-off experimental research prototypes (these should still follow coding and security baselines).

Principles

1. Predictability: APIs and deployments should behave consistently across hosted, dedicated, and private modes.
2. Observability-first: instrument before you need it: metrics, traces, logs with correlation IDs.
3. Performance-by-default: aim for efficient defaults (batching, caching, sensible quantization) and surface trade-offs.
4. Minimal blast radius: safe defaults, feature flags, canary rollouts, and fallbacks.
5. Repeatability: infra as code (Terraform), documented runbooks, and reproducible builds.

1) API Standards

Purpose: Ensure interoperable, stable, and predictable APIs across Redwood's product surface (Redwood API, control plane endpoints, admin APIs).

Key rules:
- Style: RESTful JSON over HTTPS for customer-facing APIs; gRPC allowed for internal high-throughput links with a clear contract.
- Versioning: Use semantic path versioning: /v1/, /v2/. Breaking changes require ADR + migration plan and at least one release cycle of backwards-compatibility support.
- Resource naming: kebab-case for endpoints (e.g., /model-variants).
- Request/response schema: JSON Schema for REST; protobufs for gRPC. All schemas must be published to the internal schema registry.
- Pagination: cursor-based (opaque tokens).
- Error handling: follow RFC 7807 Problem Details pattern. Include machine-readable error_code, user_message, and docs_url.
- Rate limiting and quotas: document per-endpoint default rate limits in the API reference. Throttling responses must return 429 and Retry-After.
- Authentication/Authorization: JWT bearer tokens for hosted endpoints; mTLS for internal service-to-service where applicable. RBAC rules must be declared in the service manifest.

Example (problem details):
{
  "type": "https://redwood.ai/docs/errors#quota_exceeded",
  "title": "Quota exceeded",
  "status": 429,
  "error_code": "quota_exceeded",
  "user_message": "You have exceeded your request quota for this period.",
  "docs_url": "/docs/api/quotas"
}

2) Coding Standards

- Languages: Primary services use Go (backend infra), Python (evals & ML infra), and TypeScript (console/frontend). Exceptions require engineering lead approval.
- Style & formatting: Apply gofmt/black/prettier on commit via CI.
- Linters: golangci-lint (Go), pylint/ruff (Python), ESLint/TypeScript. Fail CI on new high/critical lint errors.
- Dependencies: Use dependency-review for PRs that update transitive deps. No direct use of unvetted native extensions without security review.
- Testing: Unit tests + integration tests covering the critical code paths. Services must include a test harness that can be run in CI with mocked downstreams. Maintain >= 80% coverage on critical packages (serving, auth, routing).
- Logging: Structured JSON logs with these standard fields: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, user_id (if applicable), trace_id, msg. Avoid PII in logs.
- Secrets: Never commit secrets. Use KMS-integrated secrets manager and reference via environment-injected variables.

3) Infrastructure Standards

- IaC: Terraform modules in terraform/enterprise-modules. All production infra changes must go through Terraform with plan + peer review.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. Staging must mirror prod networking and capacity ratios (min 70%).
- Networking: Zero-trust by default (least privilege security groups, service ingress only via API gateway or internal LB). Use VPC peering / private endpoints for Private deployment connectivity.
- IAM: Principle of least privilege; roles reviewed quarterly. Use short-lived credentials for automation where possible.
- Secrets and KMS: Use cloud KMS + HSM for customer-managed keys in Private deployments. Key rotation policy: rotate root keys annually, API signing keys every 90 days.
- Disaster recovery: Daily snapshots for critical stateful services, RTO/RPO documented per service.

Configuration table (examples):
| Component | Terraform Module | Default Region | Drift Detection | Backup RPO |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Control Plane DB | tf/control-plane-db | us-west-2 | daily | 24h |
| Serving GPU Pool | tf/serving-gpu-pool | us-west-2 | hourly | 4h |

4) Model-serving Standards

- Packaging: Models must ship with a standardized manifest (model.json) containing model_id, architecture, tokenizer_spec, quantization_profile, and required runtime flags.
- Versioning: Immutable model artifacts with semantic version tags. Model registry holds metadata and SRI hashes.
- Quantization: Certified quantization profiles live in confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles. Any quantization that changes model semantics requires an eval against the approved prompt set.
- KV cache & state: Transparent cache semantics must be documented; caches should support TTLs and eviction policies. Expose cache hit/miss metrics.
- Memory & GPU limits: Each model variant includes recommended max sequence length, peak GPU memory usage estimate, and per-request KV footprint. Autoscaling policies must be dimensioned against these numbers.
- Fallbacks: Services must define at least one fallback strategy for capacity or model-quality failures (e.g., lower-cost variant, shorter max tokens, or degraded feature flag).

Model manifest example (JSON snippet):
{
  "model_id": "llama-3-13b-v1",
  "arch": "decoder-only",
  "tokenizer": "sentencepiece-1.0",
  "quant_profile": "int8-default",
  "max_seq": 4096
}

5) Observability Standards

- Metrics: Use Prometheus-compatible metrics. Standard metrics per service: request_count, request_latency_seconds (histogram), request_errors_total, downstream_latency_seconds, model_kv_cache_hits_total, model_kv_cache_misses_total.
- Tracing: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry. All entry points must propagate trace_id and span_id. Sample rate: 1% default; 100% for error traces and selected Canary runs.
- Logs: Centralized ELK/observability cluster. Logs must be indexed by service, env, request_id, trace_id.
- Dashboards: Every service must ship at least 3 dashboards: overview (traffic & errors), performance (latency & throughput), and capacity (utilization & queueing).
- Alerts & SLOs: Define SLOs per service (see Performance Standards). Alerts must map to runbooks and include paging thresholds for on-call teams.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

Default SLOs (customer-facing generation endpoints):
| Metric | Target | SLO Window | Error Budget |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| P95 latency (single-token tail) | <= 120 ms | 30d | 0.2% |
| P99 latency | <= 350 ms | 30d | 0.5% |
| Availability | >= 99.9% | 30d | 0.1% |

Notes and tuning:
- Use batching and autoscaling to preserve P95 while meeting throughput targets.
- Continuous KV prefix caching is recommended for low-latency repeated prefixes.
- For Dedicated customers with reserved throughput, negotiate bespoke SLOs in the contract and record in the product requirements.

Performance playbook (high-level steps):
1. Verify the incident with observability dashboards and request traces.
2. Run perf benchmarks in the benchmarking suite to isolate regression (compare against baseline images in /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite).
3. If regression is model-side, trigger a model rollback or canary to a verified variant.
4. If infra-side, scale GPU pools or roll a hotfix.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process

Purpose: Provide a lightweight, discoverable history of architecture decisions that affect cross-team compatibility, cost, security, and customer experience.

When to create an ADR:
- Any breaking API change.
- Selecting a major infrastructure component (e.g., new orchestration system, new networking model for Private deployments).
- Changes to model-serving semantics that affect output or latency.
- Any decision that will be referenced in support/debugging or legal/compliance reviews.

ADR Template (must be created as a confluence doc and recorded in arch ADR index):
- Title (short)
- Status (proposed | accepted | deprecated)
- Date
- Authors
- Context (background and constraints)
- Decision (what we will do)
- Consequences (positive and negative)
- Rollout plan and migration steps
- Related pages / links

ADR lifecycle steps (numbered):
1. Draft ADR in architecture-and-standards/decision-records with authors and reviewers.
2. Peer review by impacted teams (SRE, Platform, Serving, Security).
3. Present in weekly Architecture Review meeting or asynchronously if minor.
4. Record acceptance and update related runbooks, schemas, and roadmaps.
5. If deprecated, create a follow-up ADR documenting migration.

Sample ADR index entry (table):
| ADR ID | Title | Status | Date | Owner | Link |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| ADR-2026-01 | Unified API Versioning Strategy | accepted | 2026-01-05 | Aisha Patel | /architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-2026-01 |

8) Rollout & Change Management

- Canary policy: Default 5% traffic for 24 hours with 0 errors allowed for critical endpoints. Increase in doubling steps (5%, 20%, 50%, 100%) only after health checks pass for at least 2 monitoring windows.
- Feature flags: Use the central flags service. All behavioral changes must be behind a flag for a minimum of one release cycle.
- Communication: Major infra or API changes must be announced in #eng-announce and the Product/Support channels, with migration docs and an approved rollback plan.

9) Ownership & Governance

- Document owners: Each page must list a service owner and an on-call rotation for infra-critical runbooks.
- Standards board: Quarterly architecture review board (platform + runtime + security + product) will approve cross-cutting standard changes.

Appendix: Useful links
- Model quantization profiles: /applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles
- Perf suite: /eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- ADR directory: /architecture-and-standards/decision-records
- Terraform modules: /eng-infra/terraform-and-iac
